EXT. BANNOCK HARBOR - NIGHT

The MARGARET ROSE rides at anchor in the outer harbor, dark against a darker sky. Along the seawall, the whole town has turned out, candles cupped in fists against the breeze.

A Boston Whaler skiff crosses the black water. Danny at the tiller. Mara amidships with the urn in her lap. Sam in the bow in a life vest two sizes too big, one hand knotted in Barnacle's collar. The old dog rides like a figurehead, nose into the wind.

They come alongside the Margaret Rose. Danny and Mara climb aboard; Sam and the dog stay in the skiff, holding the rail.

INT./EXT. MARGARET ROSE - WHEELHOUSE - NIGHT - CONTINUOUS

Mara sets the urn on the chart shelf, where the coffee thermos rode for forty years. Danny lashes it fast with a dock line, cinches it, tests it.

Mara lifts the old brass compass out of its gimbal and pockets it. Danny sees. Says nothing.

DANNY
(handing her the flare gun)
You do it.

MARA
Why me?

DANNY
He decided you belonged here. So you do.

EXT. BANNOCK HARBOR - NIGHT - CONTINUOUS

They drop back into the skiff and stand off, engine idling, the radio crackling once with nothing.

Mara stands, braces, and fires the flare into the soaked blankets amidships.

WHUMP. A line of blue-orange flame walks the deck like it knows the boat. Then the diesel catches and the MARGARET ROSE goes up -- a column of fire standing on the black water, doubled in the swell, huge.

On the seawall, a hundred candle-flames and one enormous gasp. Then, from speakers somebody has rigged on the seawall railing, Buckley's "Hallelujah" starts again, drifting out across the water toward the fire.

Crow touches a road flare to the mortar fuse. The Fourth of July stash goes up -- white and gold chrysanthemums blooming over the burning boat, reflections shattering across the harbor.

Sam stands up in the skiff for a better look.

DANNY
Sit DOWN --

Sam sits. Barnacle barks at the fireworks, once, on principle.

Then -- a CRACK from the fire. The anchor line, burned through at the chock, parts. The burning boat swings free and begins to drift, slow and terrible, on the last of the tide.

Toward a row of moored floats. The nearest one flying a little pennant: HENDERSON.

MARA
You have got to be kidding me.

Before Danny can speak she has the spare line over her shoulder and she DIVES -- off the skiff into the black water, surfacing in the firelight, swimming hard for the mooring buoy off the Margaret Rose's bow.

DANNY
MARA!

She reaches the buoy, gets the line through the eye with numb hands, waves. Danny throws the skiff into gear, takes up the slack, and eases the burning boat's head around -- slow, straining, the flames roaring overhead -- until the drift points at open water.

He swings back and hauls Mara over the gunwale, soaked, gasping, shaking with cold and adrenaline and something else entirely.

DANNY (CONT'D)
You're insane. You know that. That was --
(laughing, despite everything)
-- that was fucking beautiful.

MARA
(through chattering teeth)
He would have HATED hitting the Hendersons'.

Out in the dark, the MARGARET ROSE burns down to the waterline, going out the way a day goes out, while Buckley's voice carries over the water and the last fireworks fall.

state.script_text:
Title: SLACK TIDE
Credit: written by
Author: The GREENLIGHT Team
Draft date: 2026-08-24
Notes: Original work. Written as the demo fixture for GREENLIGHT. All characters and the town of Port Bannock are fictional.

FADE IN:

EXT. PORT BANNOCK HARBOR - DAWN

Fog sits on the water like it pays rent. Lobster boats nod against their moorings. Somewhere a halyard clinks against a mast, patient as a clock.

A rental sedan rolls to a stop at the head of the town pier. MARA VOSS (38), city coat, wrong shoes for a dock, sits with both hands on the wheel long after the engine dies.

Through the windshield: a lobster boat rides alone on its mooring, hull the green of old bottles. Stenciled across the transom: MARGARET ROSE.

Mara looks at the boat the way you look at a photograph of yourself as a child.

MARA
(quiet)
Hey, old man.

She gets out. Gulls wheel and holler. The fog takes no notice of her at all.

INT. THE WHEELHOUSE - DAY

A harbor bar that hasn't changed since the Carter administration and is proud of it. Buoys on the ceiling. A woodstove. The smell of beer and diesel and forty years of wet wool.

On the wall: a sun-bleached framed print of Edward Hopper's NIGHTHAWKS, hanging slightly crooked. Behind the register, thumbtacked and curling: a Polaroid of a younger ELI VOSS arm-wrestling BRUCE SPRINGSTEEN, both of them laughing, "1988" in ballpoint across the white strip. Beside it, framed: a front page of the Gloucester Daily Times -- "BANNOCK CAPTAIN PULLS FOUR FROM NOR'EASTER."

On the corner TV, muted, an old VHS of JAWS is playing. The shark is winning.

DANNY VOSS (34) stands behind the bar, not because he works there but because standing anywhere else feels wrong today. SAM (10) sits at the end of the bar doing serious damage to a cocoa, poured from a dented Thermos.

CROW (60s, foul-weather bibs, a face like a chart of bad decisions) nurses a beer he transparently hates. Across his forearm, a full-rigged schooner tattoo in fading blue-black — Teddy Krane's design, inked at his Rockland parlor the summer the Margaret Rose launched — rides every pour like weather.

CROW
Thirty years I drank whatever Eli stocked, out of loyalty. Coors Light. Tastes like a wet napkin. Man ran the best bar on this coast and drank the worst beer in America.

DANNY
He liked that it was cheap.

CROW
He liked that it annoyed me.

The door opens. Mara stands in it with a duffel bag. The room goes quiet the way only a small town can go quiet -- all at once, and politely.

DANNY (CONT'D)
You came.

MARA
He died.

DANNY
People have died before. You didn't come.

A beat. Sam slides off his stool, crosses to Mara, and offers up the Thermos cup like a church collection.

SAM
Aunt Mara. Want some? Dad made it with water, though. I'm supposed to say that first.

MARA
(taking the stool beside him)
Then absolutely not.

Sam grins. Something in the room loosens a notch.

HELEN FITCH (60s, funeral director, cardigan over steel) comes in from the back room carrying a manila envelope like it might go off.

HELEN
Good. You're both here. He left instructions. Notarized. Which, for Eli Voss, is close to a miracle.

She hands the envelope to Danny. He opens it, unfolds a single handwritten page, and reads.

DANNY
(reading)
"One. No church-basement sandwiches. Real food. If there is a casserole in that building I will know."

CROW
Fair.

DANNY
(reading)
"Two. At the service, play 'Hallelujah.' The Jeff Buckley one. The Columbia recording. Not a cover. Not your cousin with the ukulele. Buckley, or nothing."

HELEN
And three?

Danny reads ahead silently. Stops. Reads it again.

DANNY
(reading)
"Three. Burn the boat. With me on it. At slack tide, so I don't drift into the Hendersons' float again."

Silence. Crow raises the terrible beer.

CROW
Viking.

MARA
He cannot be serious. You can't just burn a boat in the harbor.

CROW
You can if you don't ask first.

EXT. TOWN PIER - NIGHT

Low tide. The pilings stand up out of the mud like the legs of something huge and patient. Mara and Danny sit on the pier's end with their feet hanging over black water.

Danny produces a joint, lights it, offers it over. Mara stares at it.

DANNY
Since when do you not?

MARA
Since I bill by the hour.

She takes it anyway. A long drag. She holds it like an old phone number she's surprised she still knows.

Out of the dark comes BARNACLE, an ancient black Lab with a gray muzzle and the gait of a sea captain on land. He flops down between them with a groan and puts his head on Mara's knee.

MARA (CONT'D)
He kept the dog.

DANNY
The dog kept him. There's a difference.

They pass the joint. Water slaps the pilings.

DANNY (CONT'D)
You remember Fenway? He hears on the radio the game's a sellout, so obviously that's the day we're going. No tickets. Walks us past the gate guy carrying a clipboard he took off a wall. "Walk like you own the place." We saw the whole game from the standing rail.

MARA
(laughing despite herself)
He made us wave at the camera like we belonged there.

DANNY
We did belong there. That was the trick. He decided we belonged, so we did.

The laugh drains out of her.

MARA
He was a selfish, glorious, fucking impossible man, and I moved four hundred miles away to stop auditioning for him, and it didn't work. It never worked.

DANNY
(quiet)
He kept every clipping. Every case you won that made a paper, it went up behind the register. He'd tell strangers. Strangers, Mara. He never told you because you'd have won the argument about it, and he couldn't stand losing twice.

Mara looks at the water for a long time. Barnacle sighs like a man twice his age.

INT. ST. BRIGID'S CHURCH - DAY

Full pews. Fishermen in blazers that fit them two funerals ago. The casket at the front under a spray of lilies and, at Helen's visible disapproval, a coiled dock line.

At the side of the altar, an honor guard: three OLD VETERANS in dress uniforms, service rifles held at rest, faces like the granite outside.

Crow walks to the front. No accompanist. He grips the lectern, and into the dead-quiet room he sings -- rough, unhurried, surprisingly tender -- the old Stephen Foster hymn "Hard Times Come Again No More."

CROW
(singing)
'Tis the song, the sigh of the weary. Hard times, hard times, come again no more...

Nobody breathes. He finishes. He nods once, to the casket, like closing a bar tab, and sits.

Helen steps up. She sets a battered BOOMBOX on the altar rail, and looks at it with naked distrust. Sam, in the front pew, gives her a thumbs up.

She presses play.

The opening guitar of Jeff Buckley's "Hallelujah" -- the Columbia recording, unmistakable, that lone electric guitar in a big empty room -- fills the church.

Hold on the faces. Danny's jaw working. Sam mouthing the words. Mara, eyes forward, absolutely still, tears moving anyway.

EXT. ST. BRIGID'S CHURCHYARD - DAY

The mourners in a loose crescent under a pewter sky. The honor guard stands in a row, rifles up at the ready.

VETERAN
Ready. Aim. Fire.

VOLLEY. Gulls explode off the church roof. Sam clamps his hands over his ears. Barnacle, tied to the fence, points his muzzle at the sky and HOWLS.

VOLLEY. VOLLEY.

The senior veteran presents the folded flag -- not to Danny, not to Mara. To Sam. The boy takes it like it weighs a hundred pounds, because it does.

INT. THE WHEELHOUSE - DAY

THE WAKE. The bar packed to the walls. Chowder in mismatched bowls. Real food; no sandwiches in sight. Laughter in that specific register that lives one door down from crying.

At the bar, COUSIN TEDDY (40s, tie loosened, several drinks ahead of the room) holds forth.

TEDDY
All I'm saying -- all I'm saying is that boat surveys at forty grand, and the plan is to torch it. That's the estate. That's my family's --

DANNY
Say that again.

TEDDY
It's a boat, Danny. He was a drunk with a fucking boat, and you're all acting like it's the crown jewels.

You remember Fenway? He hears on the radio the game's a sellout, so obviously that's the day we're going. No tickets. Walks us past the gate guy carrying a clipboard he took off a wall. "Walk like you own the place." We saw the whole game from the standing rail.

MARA
(laughing despite herself)
He made us wave at the camera like we belonged there.

DANNY
We did belong there. That was the trick. He decided we belonged, so we did.

The laugh drains out of her.

MARA
He was a selfish, glorious, fucking impossible man, and I moved four hundred miles away to stop auditioning for him, and it didn't work. It never worked.

DANNY
(quiet)
He kept every clipping. Every case you won that made a paper, it went up behind the register. He'd tell strangers. Strangers, Mara. He never told you because you'd have won the argument about it, and he couldn't stand losing twice.

Mara looks at the water for a long time. Barnacle sighs like a man twice his age.

[S004] INT. ST. BRIGID'S CHURCH - DAY

Full pews. Fishermen in blazers that fit them two funerals ago. The casket at the front under a spray of lilies and, at Helen's visible disapproval, a coiled dock line.

At the side of the altar, an honor guard: three OLD VETERANS in dress uniforms, service rifles held at rest, faces like the granite outside.

Crow walks to the front. No accompanist. He grips the lectern, and into the dead-quiet room he sings -- rough, unhurried, surprisingly tender -- the old Stephen Foster hymn "Hard Times Come Again No More."

CROW
(singing)
'Tis the song, the sigh of the weary. Hard times, hard times, come again no more...

Nobody breathes. He finishes. He nods once, to the casket, like closing a bar tab, and sits.

Helen steps up. She sets a battered BOOMBOX on the altar rail, and looks at it with naked distrust. Sam, in the front pew, gives her a thumbs up.

She presses play.

The opening guitar of Jeff Buckley's "Hallelujah" -- the Columbia recording, unmistakable, that lone electric guitar in a big empty room -- fills the church.

Hold on the faces. Danny's jaw working. Sam mouthing the words. Mara, eyes forward, absolutely still, tears moving anyway.

[S005] EXT. ST. BRIGID'S CHURCHYARD - DAY

The mourners in a loose crescent under a pewter sky. The honor guard stands in a row, rifles up at the ready.

VETERAN
Ready. Aim. Fire.

VOLLEY. Gulls explode off the church roof. Sam clamps his hands over his ears. Barnacle, tied to the fence, points his muzzle at the sky and HOWLS.

VOLLEY. VOLLEY.

The senior veteran presents the folded flag -- not to Danny, not to Mara. To Sam. The boy takes it like it weighs a hundred pounds, because it does.

[S006] INT. THE WHEELHOUSE - DAY

THE WAKE. The bar packed to the walls. Chowder in mismatched bowls. Real food; no sandwiches in sight. Laughter in that specific register that lives one door down from crying.

At the bar, COUSIN TEDDY (40s, tie loosened, several drinks ahead of the room) holds forth.

TEDDY
All I'm saying -- all I'm saying is that boat surveys at forty grand, and the plan is to torch it. That's the estate. That's my family's --

DANNY
Say that again.

TEDDY
It's a boat, Danny. He was a drunk with a fucking boat, and you're all acting like it's the crown jewels.

Danny hits him. One punch, no windup, the kind you learn on a working dock.

Teddy goes back over a stool and comes up swinging, and for five ugly seconds it is a real fight -- grappling, a glass shattering, blood bright from Teddy's nose across the bar top -- before Crow peels them apart with an ease that suggests long practice.

CROW
(to Teddy, mild)
Go home, Ted. Tide's going out. Try and go with it.

Helen is already there with a stack of cocktail napkins, dressing Teddy's nose with the brisk efficiency of a corner cutman. Mara surveys the wreckage.

MARA
(to Helen)
"Real food, no sandwiches, and a fistfight." He got everything he asked for.

HELEN
They usually do.

[S007] INT. THE WHEELHOUSE - NIGHT

Long after. Empty. Chairs up on tables. One lamp behind the bar. Mara alone, counting the night's take, not counting it at all.

She takes down the good whiskey from the top shelf -- the bottle no one is allowed to touch -- and pours two glasses. Sets one at the far end of the bar. Old habit. She doesn't seem to notice she's done it.

ELI VOSS (70) is sitting in front of the far glass. Work jacket. Salt-white stubble. He was not there a moment ago, and the room does not find this strange.

ELI
You put the Hopper crooked.

Mara does not turn around. Her hands go still on the register.

ELI (CONT'D)
It's been crooked eleven years. But you looked at it tonight, so now it's your fault.

MARA
(not turning)
You're not here.

ELI
I'm not anywhere. It's very freeing. No tide chart. No Coors Light.

MARA
(turning now)
That you drank on purpose. For thirty years. Out of spite.

ELI
Loyalty. Spite is just loyalty with the brights on.

She comes down the bar. Stops an arm's length away. Up close he is exactly himself: unhurried, amused, infuriating.

MARA
I came back four times. Ma's funeral. Danny's wedding. Twice more. You talked to me about bilge pumps.

ELI
I know.

MARA
That's it? You know?

ELI
You were the one thing I ever made that didn't need fixing. I didn't have a language for that. Bilge pumps, I had.

Mara's eyes fill. She hates it. She lets it happen anyway.

MARA
The boat's worth fifty thousand dollars, Dad.

ELI
The boat is a coffin with a diesel in it. Everything I loved either walked off it or died on it, except you, and you swam.
(beat)
Burn it, Mare. Stand on the seawall with your brother and watch it go, and be done carrying it.

MARA
(barely)
Slack tide?

ELI
Slack tide. I meant that part. The Hendersons have suffered enough.

She laughs -- an ugly, wet, wonderful laugh. She wipes her eyes with the heel of her hand, and when she looks up the stool is empty.

At the far end of the bar, his glass is empty too.

[S008] EXT. BANNOCK BOATYARD - DAY

The MARGARET ROSE up on stands, Danny and Crow moving over her with jerry cans of diesel, soaking coiled blankets along the deck. It is exactly as legal as it looks.

Crow lugs a milk crate aboard: cardboard tubes, mortar shells, a coil of fuse.

CROW
Fourth of July stash. Three years of it. He'd want the good ones up.

A white pickup with U.S. Coast Guard markings rolls into the yard. PETTY OFFICER REYES (30s, squared away, unreadable) steps out and takes a long look at the diesel cans, the blankets, the fireworks, and the two men standing in front of them like boys caught smoking.

REYES
Mr. Voss. Word around the harbor is you're planning a marine event. Open flame, on a vessel, in navigable waters. I checked. There's no permit on file.

DANNY
It's a funeral.

REYES
It's an unpermitted burn with a homemade pyrotechnics display, is what it is.

A long silence. Reyes looks past them, at the boat's transom. MARGARET ROSE.

REYES (CONT'D)
Eli Voss pulled my mother out of the water in 'ninety-eight. Her and three others, in a following sea, in a boat half this size.
(beat)
Slack tide's at nine-forty. My patrol ends at nine. Keep it in the outer harbor, keep a skiff standing off with a radio, and keep that boy of yours in a life jacket.

He gets back in the truck. Rolls the window down.

REYES (CONT'D)
I was never here.

DANNY
Never where?

The truck pulls out. Crow watches it go.

CROW
I like her.

[S009] EXT. BANNOCK HARBOR - NIGHT

The MARGARET ROSE rides at anchor in the outer harbor, dark against a darker sky. Along the seawall, the whole town has turned out, candles cupped in fists against the breeze.

A Boston Whaler skiff crosses the black water. Danny at the tiller. Mara amidships with the urn in her lap. Sam in the bow in a life vest two sizes too big, one hand knotted in Barnacle's collar. The old dog rides like a figurehead, nose into the wind.

They come alongside the Margaret Rose. Danny and Mara climb aboard; Sam and the dog stay in the skiff, holding the rail.

[S010] INT./EXT. MARGARET ROSE - WHEELHOUSE - NIGHT - CONTINUOUS

Mara sets the urn on the chart shelf, where the coffee thermos rode for forty years. Danny lashes it fast with a dock line, cinches it, tests it.

Mara lifts the old brass compass out of its gimbal and pockets it. Danny sees. Says nothing.

DANNY
(handing her the flare gun)
You do it.

MARA
Why me?

DANNY
He decided you belonged here. So you do.

[S011] EXT. BANNOCK HARBOR - NIGHT - CONTINUOUS

They drop back into the skiff and stand off, engine idling, the radio crackling once with nothing.

Mara stands, braces, and fires the flare into the soaked blankets amidships.

WHUMP. A line of blue-orange flame walks the deck like it knows the boat. Then the diesel catches and the MARGARET ROSE goes up -- a column of fire standing on the black water, doubled in the swell, huge.

On the seawall, a hundred candle-flames and one enormous gasp. Then, from speakers somebody has rigged on the seawall railing, Buckley's "Hallelujah" starts again, drifting out across the water toward the fire.

Crow touches a road flare to the mortar fuse. The Fourth of July stash goes up -- white and gold chrysanthemums blooming over the burning boat, reflections shattering across the harbor.

Sam stands up in the skiff for a better look.

DANNY
Sit DOWN --

Sam sits. Barnacle barks at the fireworks, once, on principle.

Then -- a CRACK from the fire. The anchor line, burned through at the chock, parts. The burning boat swings free and begins to drift, slow and terrible, on the last of the tide.

Toward a row of moored floats. The nearest one flying a little pennant: HENDERSON.

MARA
You have got to be kidding me.

Before Danny can speak she has the spare line over her shoulder and she DIVES -- off the skiff into the black water, surfacing in the firelight, swimming hard for the mooring buoy off the Margaret Rose's bow.

DANNY
MARA!

She reaches the buoy, gets the line through the eye with numb hands, waves. Danny throws the skiff into gear, takes up the slack, and eases the burning boat's head around -- slow, straining, the flames roaring overhead -- until the drift points at open water.

He swings back and hauls Mara over the gunwale, soaked, gasping, shaking with cold and adrenaline and something else entirely.

DANNY (CONT'D)
You're insane. You know that. That was --
(laughing, despite everything)
-- that was fucking beautiful.

MARA
(through chattering teeth)
He would have HATED hitting the Hendersons'.

Out in the dark, the MARGARET ROSE burns down to the waterline, going out the way a day goes out, while Buckley's voice carries over the water and the last fireworks fall.

[S012] EXT. STONE JETTY - DAWN

Flat calm. The fog is back, gentler now. Ash rides the tideline like gray lace.

Mara and Danny sit on the rocks with coffee, passing the dented Thermos cup between them. Barnacle lies across Mara's feet, asleep with his eyes open, the way old dogs and old sailors do.

Sam walks the tideline below them, the folded flag still under his arm. He hasn't put it down since the churchyard.

DANNY
You heading back Sunday?

Mara turns the brass compass over in her hands. The needle finds north, patient as ever.

MARA
Eventually.

Danny nods. That's enough. That's plenty.

Out on the empty water, the mooring where the MARGARET ROSE rode for forty years holds nothing at all. A gull lands on the buoy, decides it's not worth the trouble, and lifts away into the fog.

FADE OUT.

excerpts: The following procedures are recommended for all water work, including, but not limited to: ponds, rivers, lakes, swamps, bogs, oceans, pools, and tanks, or any other unduly wet work environment.

flags:safety_underwriter.finding: Scenes S009, S010, and S011 depict a heavily stacked sequence of physical hazards taking place in open harbor waters at night. The staged action includes discharging a flare gun into fuel-soaked blankets on an anchored vessel (Margaret Rose), causing an engulfing fire and diesel burn, adjacent aerial mortar fireworks launched from the seawall, a severed anchor line causing the burning vessel to drift toward moored floats, a character (Mara) diving into cold water at night to swim a line to a mooring buoy, boat maneuvers adjacent to flames to tow the vessel, and an adjacent skiff carrying a child character (Sam) and a dog (Barnacle). These stacked hazards compound fire/pyrotechnics, cold-water immersion, night vessel operations, and vulnerable character presence. While the script depicts these story events, practical versus visual effects execution, shooting jurisdiction, casting ages, and marine safety protocols remain unconfirmed production decisions.

citations.title: CSATF Safety Bulletin #16: Recommended Guidelines for Safety with Pyrotechnic Special Effects
citations.excerpt: When pyrotechnic materials are used on set, such use shall be under controlled conditions with due regard for the safety of all involved. • The Production Company or Studio shall make sufficient advanced notification of the use of pyrotechnic materials to the appropriate departments (such as Special Effects, Stunts, Camera, Art, Construction, Hair, Make-up and Wardrobe), in order to safely plan pyrotechnic special effects. Any performer who may be involved in a pyrotechnic special effect shall be notified. • Any required licenses and/or permits shall be obtained from proper Authorities Having Jurisdiction (AHJ) over pyrotechnic materials prior to using pyrotechnic special effects. Pyrotechnic Special Effects Operator(s) must hold valid State and Federal license(s), as applicable.

remedy.detail: 1. Pyrotechnics & Fire: If practical fire, flare discharge, or fireworks are utilized, engage a licensed Pyrotechnic Special Effects Operator and obtain required permits from the Authority Having Jurisdiction (AHJ) in compliance with CSATF Safety Bulletin #16; alternatively, execute the vessel burn, flare ignition, and mortar fireworks using CGI/VFX or controlled tank/miniature elements to eliminate live open-water fire hazards. 2. Marine & Water Safety: For practical night water work and the depicted swimming stunt, engage a Marine Coordinator and dedicated Water Safety / Lifesaving personnel per CSATF Safety Bulletin #17 and #15. Provide appropriate personal flotation devices, buddy/personnel accounting systems, qualified stunt doubles for the dive and tow sequence, and active hypothermia mitigation measures (including warm staging areas/tents, heated dry suits or thermal layers, and immediate medical standby). 3. Minor and Animal Staging: Confirm performer casting age and animal handling plans; if a minor performer or live animal is cast, enforce jurisdictional minor working hours and welfare safeguards, provide certified animal handler supervision per CSATF Safety Bulletin #6, or stage the child and animal elements separately from night water and pyrotechnic filming via plates/split-screen. Schedule and cost estimates are omitted as they depend on the chosen shooting location, marine logistics, and practical versus VFX method determinations.

scenes.heading: EXT. PORT BANNOCK HARBOR - DAWN
scenes.action:
Fog sits on the water like it pays rent. Lobster boats nod against their moorings. Somewhere a halyard clinks against a mast, patient as a clock.

A rental sedan rolls to a stop at the head of the town pier. MARA VOSS (38), city coat, wrong shoes for a dock, sits with both hands on the wheel long after the engine dies.

Through the windshield: a lobster boat rides alone on its mooring, hull the green of old bottles. Stenciled across the transom: MARGARET ROSE.

Mara looks at the boat the way you look at a photograph of yourself as a child.

She gets out. Gulls wheel and holler. The fog takes no notice of her at all.

dialogue.line: Hey, old man.

scenes.heading: INT. THE WHEELHOUSE - DAY
scenes.action:
A harbor bar that hasn't changed since the Carter administration and is proud of it. Buoys on the ceiling. A woodstove. The smell of beer and diesel and forty years of wet wool.

On the wall: a sun-bleached framed print of Edward Hopper's NIGHTHAWKS, hanging slightly crooked. Behind the register, thumbtacked and curling: a Polaroid of a younger ELI VOSS arm-wrestling BRUCE SPRINGSTEEN, both of them laughing, "1988" in ballpoint across the white strip. Beside it, framed: a front page of the Gloucester Daily Times -- "BANNOCK CAPTAIN PULLS FOUR FROM NOR'EASTER."

On the corner TV, muted, an old VHS of JAWS is playing. The shark is winning.

DANNY VOSS (34) stands behind the bar, not because he works there but because standing anywhere else feels wrong today. SAM (10) sits at the end of the bar doing serious damage to a cocoa, poured from a dented Thermos.

CROW (60s, foul-weather bibs, a face like a chart of bad decisions) nurses a beer he transparently hates. Across his forearm, a full-rigged schooner tattoo in fading blue-black — Teddy Krane's design, inked at his Rockland parlor the summer the Margaret Rose launched — rides every pour like weather.

The door opens. Mara stands in it with a duffel bag. The room goes quiet the way only a small town can go quiet -- all at once, and politely.

A beat. Sam slides off his stool, crosses to Mara, and offers up the Thermos cup like a church collection.

Sam grins. Something in the room loosens a notch.

HELEN FITCH (60s, funeral director, cardigan over steel) comes in from the back room carrying a manila envelope like it might go off.

She hands the envelope to Danny. He opens it, unfolds a single handwritten page, and reads.

Danny reads ahead silently. Stops. Reads it again.

Silence. Crow raises the terrible beer.

dialogue.line: Thirty years I drank whatever Eli stocked, out of loyalty. Coors Light. Tastes like a wet napkin. Man ran the best bar on this coast and drank the worst beer in America.
He liked that it was cheap.
He liked that it annoyed me.
You came.
He died.
People have died before. You didn't come.
Aunt Mara. Want some? Dad made it with water, though. I'm supposed to say that first.
Then absolutely not.
Good. You're both here. He left instructions. Notarized. Which, for Eli Voss, is close to a miracle.
"One. No church-basement sandwiches. Real food. If there is a casserole in that building I will know."
Fair.
"Two. At the service, play 'Hallelujah.' The Jeff Buckley one. The Columbia recording. Not a cover. Not your cousin with the ukulele. Buckley, or nothing."
And three?
"Three. Burn the boat. With me on it. At slack tide, so I don't drift into the Hendersons' float again."
Viking.
He cannot be serious. You can't just burn a boat in the harbor.
You can if you don't ask first.

scenes.heading: EXT. TOWN PIER - NIGHT
scenes.action:
Low tide. The pilings stand up out of the mud like the legs of something huge and patient. Mara and Danny sit on the pier's end with their feet hanging over black water.

Danny produces a joint, lights it, offers it over. Mara stares at it.

She takes it anyway. A long drag. She holds it like an old phone number she's surprised she still knows.

Out of the dark comes BARNACLE, an ancient black Lab with a gray muzzle and the gait of a sea captain on land. He flops down between them with a groan and puts his head on Mara's knee.

They pass the joint. Water slaps the pilings.

The laugh drains out of her.

Mara looks at the water for a long time. Barnacle sighs like a man twice his age.

dialogue.line: Since when do you not?
Since I bill by the hour.
He kept the dog.
The dog kept him. There's a difference.

You remember Fenway? He hears on the radio the game's a sellout, so obviously that's the day we're going. No tickets. Walks us past the gate guy carrying a clipboard he took off a wall. "Walk like you own the place." We saw the whole game from the standing rail.
He made us wave at the camera like we belonged there.
We did belong there. That was the trick. He decided we belonged, so we did.
He was a selfish, glorious, fucking impossible man, and I moved four hundred miles away to stop auditioning for him, and it didn't work. It never worked.

He kept every clipping. Every case you won that made a paper, it went up behind the register. He'd tell strangers. Strangers, Mara. He never told you because you'd have won the argument about it, and he couldn't stand losing twice.

scenes.heading: INT. ST. BRIGID'S CHURCH - DAY
scenes.action:
Full pews. Fishermen in blazers that fit them two funerals ago. The casket at the front under a spray of lilies and, at Helen's visible disapproval, a coiled dock line.

At the side of the altar, an honor guard: three OLD VETERANS in dress uniforms, service rifles held at rest, faces like the granite outside.

Crow walks to the front. No accompanist. He grips the lectern, and into the dead-quiet room he sings -- rough, unhurried, surprisingly tender -- the old Stephen Foster hymn "Hard Times Come Again No More."

Nobody breathes. He finishes. He nods once, to the casket, like closing a bar tab, and sits.

Helen steps up. She sets a battered BOOMBOX on the altar rail, and looks at it with naked distrust. Sam, in the front pew, gives her a thumbs up.

She presses play.

The opening guitar of Jeff Buckley's "Hallelujah" -- the Columbia recording, unmistakable, that lone electric guitar in a big empty room -- fills the church.

Hold on the faces. Danny's jaw working. Sam mouthing the words. Mara, eyes forward, absolutely still, tears moving anyway.

dialogue.line: 'Tis the song, the sigh of the weary. Hard times, hard times, come again no more...

scenes.heading: EXT. ST. BRIGID'S CHURCHYARD - DAY
scenes.action:
The mourners in a loose crescent under a pewter sky. The honor guard stands in a row, rifles up at the ready.

VOLLEY. Gulls explode off the church roof. Sam clamps his hands over his ears. Barnacle, tied to the fence, points his muzzle at the sky and HOWLS.

VOLLEY. VOLLEY.

The senior veteran presents the folded flag -- not to Danny, not to Mara. To Sam. The boy takes it like it weighs a hundred pounds, because it does.

dialogue.line: Ready. Aim. Fire.

scenes.heading: INT. THE WHEELHOUSE - DAY
scenes.action:
THE WAKE. The bar packed to the walls. Chowder in mismatched bowls. Real food; no sandwiches in sight. Laughter in that specific register that lives one door down from crying.

At the bar, COUSIN TEDDY (40s, tie loosened, several drinks ahead of the room) holds forth.

Danny hits him. One punch, no windup, the kind you learn on a working dock.

Teddy goes back over a stool and comes up swinging, and for five ugly seconds it is a real fight -- grappling, a glass shattering, blood bright from Teddy's nose across the bar top -- before Crow peels them apart with an ease that suggests long practice.

Helen is already there with a stack of cocktail napkins, dressing Teddy's nose with the brisk efficiency of a corner cutman. Mara surveys the wreckage.

dialogue.line: All I'm saying -- all I'm saying is that boat surveys at forty grand, and the plan is to torch it. That's the estate. That's my family's --
Say that again.
It's a boat, Danny. He was a drunk with a fucking boat, and you're all acting like it's the crown jewels.
Go home, Ted. Tide's going out. Try and go with it.
"Real food, no sandwiches, and a fistfight." He got everything he asked for.
They usually do.

scenes.heading: INT. THE WHEELHOUSE - NIGHT
scenes.action:
Long after. Empty. Chairs up on tables. One lamp behind the bar. Mara alone, counting the night's take, not counting it at all.

She takes down the good whiskey from the top shelf -- the bottle no one is allowed to touch -- and pours two glasses. Sets one at the far end of the bar. Old habit. She doesn't seem to notice she's done it.

ELI VOSS (70) is sitting in front of the far glass. Work jacket. Salt-white stubble. He was not there a moment ago, and the room does not find this strange.

Mara does not turn around. Her hands go still on the register.

She comes down the bar. Stops an arm's length away. Up close he is exactly himself: unhurried, amused, infuriating.

Mara's eyes fill. She hates it. She lets it happen anyway.

She laughs -- an ugly, wet, wonderful laugh. She wipes her eyes with the heel of her hand, and when she looks up the stool is empty.

At the far end of the bar, his glass is empty too.

dialogue.line: You put the Hopper crooked.
It's been crooked eleven years. But you looked at it tonight, so now it's your fault.
You're not here.
I'm not anywhere. It's very freeing. No tide chart. No Coors Light.
That you drank on purpose. For thirty years. Out of spite.
Loyalty. Spite is just loyalty with the brights on.
I came back four times. Ma's funeral. Danny's wedding. Twice more. You talked to me about bilge pumps.
I know.
That's it? You know?
You were the one thing I ever made that didn't need fixing. I didn't have a language for that. Bilge pumps, I had.
The boat's worth fifty thousand dollars, Dad.

The boat is a coffin with a diesel in it. Everything I loved either walked off it or died on it, except you, and you swam. (beat) Burn it, Mare. Stand on the seawall with your brother and watch it go, and be done carrying it.
Slack tide?
Slack tide. I meant that part. The Hendersons have suffered enough.

scenes.heading: EXT. BANNOCK BOATYARD - DAY
scenes.action:
The MARGARET ROSE up on stands, Danny and Crow moving over her with jerry cans of diesel, soaking coiled blankets along the deck. It is exactly as legal as it looks.

Crow lugs a milk crate aboard: cardboard tubes, mortar shells, a coil of fuse.

A white pickup with U.S. Coast Guard markings rolls into the yard. PETTY OFFICER REYES (30s, squared away, unreadable) steps out and takes a long look at the diesel cans, the blankets, the fireworks, and the two men standing in front of them like boys caught smoking.

A long silence. Reyes looks past them, at the boat's transom. MARGARET ROSE.

He gets back in the truck. Rolls the window down.

The truck pulls out. Crow watches it go.

dialogue.line: Fourth of July stash. Three years of it. He'd want the good ones up.
Mr. Voss. Word around the harbor is you're planning a marine event. Open flame, on a vessel, in navigable waters. I checked. There's no permit on file.
It's a funeral.
It's an unpermitted burn with a homemade pyrotechnics display, is what it is.

Eli Voss pulled my mother out of the water in 'ninety-eight. Her and three others, in a following sea, in a boat half this size. (beat) Slack tide's at nine-forty. My patrol ends at nine. Keep it in the outer harbor, keep a skiff standing off with a radio, and keep that boy of yours in a life jacket.
I was never here.
Never where?
I like her.

scenes.heading: EXT. BANNOCK HARBOR - NIGHT
scenes.action:
The MARGARET ROSE rides at anchor in the outer harbor, dark against a darker sky. Along the seawall, the whole town has turned out, candles cupped in fists against the breeze.

A Boston Whaler skiff crosses the black water. Danny at the tiller. Mara amidships with the urn in her lap. Sam in the bow in a life vest two sizes too big, one hand knotted in Barnacle's collar. The old dog rides like a figurehead, nose into the wind.

They come alongside the Margaret Rose. Danny and Mara climb aboard; Sam and the dog stay in the skiff, holding the rail.

scenes.heading: INT./EXT. MARGARET ROSE - WHEELHOUSE - NIGHT - CONTINUOUS
scenes.action:
Mara sets the urn on the chart shelf, where the coffee thermos rode for forty years. Danny lashes it fast with a dock line, cinches it, tests it.

Mara lifts the old brass compass out of its gimbal and pockets it. Danny sees. Says nothing.

dialogue.line: You do it.
Why me?
He decided you belonged here. So you do.

scenes.heading: EXT. BANNOCK HARBOR - NIGHT - CONTINUOUS
scenes.action:
They drop back into the skiff and stand off, engine idling, the radio crackling once with nothing.

Mara stands, braces, and fires the flare into the soaked blankets amidships.

WHUMP. A line of blue-orange flame walks the deck like it knows the boat. Then the diesel catches and the MARGARET ROSE goes up -- a column of fire standing on the black water, doubled in the swell, huge.

On the seawall, a hundred candle-flames and one enormous gasp. Then, from speakers somebody has rigged on the seawall railing, Buckley's "Hallelujah" starts again, drifting out across the water toward the fire.

Crow touches a road flare to the mortar fuse. The Fourth of July stash goes up -- white and gold chrysanthemums blooming over the burning boat, reflections shattering across the harbor.

Sam stands up in the skiff for a better look.

Sam sits. Barnacle barks at the fireworks, once, on principle.

Then -- a CRACK from the fire. The anchor line, burned through at the chock, parts. The burning boat swings free and begins to drift, slow and terrible, on the last of the tide.

Toward a row of moored floats. The nearest one flying a little pennant: HENDERSON.

Before Danny can speak she has the spare line over her shoulder and she DIVES -- off the skiff into the black water, surfacing in the firelight, swimming hard for the mooring buoy off the Margaret Rose's bow.

She reaches the buoy, gets the line through the eye with numb hands, waves. Danny throws the skiff into gear, takes up the slack, and eases the burning boat's head around -- slow, straining, the flames roaring overhead -- until the drift points at open water.

He swings back and hauls Mara over the gunwale, soaked, gasping, shaking with cold and adrenaline and something else entirely.

Out in the dark, the MARGARET ROSE burns down to the waterline, going out the way a day goes out, while Buckley's voice carries over the water and the last fireworks fall.

dialogue.line: Sit DOWN --
You have got to be kidding me.
MARA!
You're insane. You know that. That was -- (laughing, despite everything) -- that was fucking beautiful.
He would have HATED hitting the Hendersons'.

scenes.heading: EXT. STONE JETTY - DAWN
scenes.action:
Flat calm. The fog is back, gentler now. Ash rides the tideline like gray lace.

Mara and Danny sit on the rocks with coffee, passing the dented Thermos cup between them. Barnacle lies across Mara's feet, asleep with his eyes open, the way old dogs and old sailors do.

Sam walks the tideline below them, the folded flag still under his arm. He hasn't put it down since the churchyard.

Mara turns the brass compass over in her hands. The needle finds north, patient as ever.

Danny nods. That's enough. That's plenty.

Out on the empty water, the mooring where the MARGARET ROSE rode for forty years holds nothing at all. A gull lands on the buoy, decides it's not worth the trouble, and lifts away into the fog.

dialogue.line: You heading back Sunday?
Eventually.

**Clothing and Personal Protective Equipment** • Cast and crew in close proximity to planned effects should wear appropriate protective clothing.
Depending on the hazards involved, this clothing should include appropriate closed-toe footwear, long pants, and a long-sleeved shirt made of 100% cotton or material which provides equal or greater protection.
• Cast and crew must be notified by the Pyrotechnic Special Effects Operator in charge when there is potential for exposures to pyrotechnics, such as fireball, debris, and shock wave. PPE must be provided as appropriate for the hazard(s) involved and considerations must be made for head, hand, eye, ear and respiratory protection.
Depending on the hazards involved, the AHJ may require full fire turnout gear and Self Contained Breathing Apparatus (SCBA). These guidelines will also apply to performers when appropriate. All users must have proper training in the use and limitations of such PPE.
**Fire Protection** • Pyrotechnic materials shall be kept a safe distance from open flames and other sources of ignition. Where required, such materials shall also be stored in approved, properly labeled containers.
• Smoking is prohibited in all pyrotechnic areas and "No Smoking" signs shall be posted in all appropriate areas of the premises or locations where pyrotechnic materials are stored and handled.
• Sufficient fire suppression equipment (such as charged extinguishers and fire hoses) must be manned, ready for use and placed at an appropriate safe distance from the effect, during testing, rehearsal and filming.
• Designated personnel performing fire suppression activities during testing, rehearsal and filming must be properly clothed and wear appropriate PPE.

**Personnel Using and Handling Pyrotechnic Materials** • Special effects personnel working with pyrotechnic materials (pyrotechnicians) should be dressed in appropriate clothing to protect them from potential hazards.
At a minimum, clothing should consist of appropriate closed-toe footwear, long pants, and a long-sleeved shirt made of 100% cotton or material which provides equal or greater protection. PPE considerations must be made for head, hand, eye, ear and respiratory protection. Depending on the hazards involved, the AHJ may require full fire turnout gear.
• Intoxicating liquids, drugs and other controlled substances (except for prescription drugs not impairing the user's judgment and motor functions) shall not be used by any person handling pyrotechnic special effects at any time during transportation, set-up, firing or removal.
• Pyrotechnicians must be given sufficient time to safely perform the work (including the transporting, storing, creating, rigging, firing, striking and extinguishing of all pyrotechnic special effects materials). While conducting such duties, pyrotechnicians should not be rushed, interrupted or distracted from focusing on their work.
• The rigging of any type of pyrotechnic device to a performer shall be done by a qualified special effects operator.
• Pyrotechnic special effects shall not be fired unless the area involved with the firing is in the continuously unobstructed full view of the Pyrotechnic Special Effects Operator in charge or his or her designated representative at the time of firing, unless equal means of observation are used.
**Awareness** • When using pyrotechnic special effects on any set, notification shall be given to personnel by way of the call sheet, or other suitable means. The call sheet should also state the type of pyrotechnic special effects work that is planned.
• Before any pyrotechnic special effects or potentially hazardous sequence is to be performed, all persons involved shall be thoroughly briefed at a safety orientation meeting on the site.
• The safety orientation meeting shall include an "on site walk-through" and/or "dry run" with the Pyrotechnic Special Effects Operator in charge and all other persons involved in the event, including Stunt Coordinator if applicable. PPE should be in place at that time.

**Use of Power Sources in Firing Pyrotechnic Materials** • To protect against accidental firing, all electrically fired pyrotechnic devices shall be shunted at all times prior to firing.
• Power sources for firing pyrotechnic special effects devices shall be restricted to isolated ungrounded batteries or individually designated ungrounded generators (below 5 kilowatts to comply with non-grounding requirements) used exclusively for firing purposes only. • Commercial or house power shall not be used directly for firing purposes.
• There should be no wireless transmissions in the area where electrically fired pyrotechnic devices are being used without prior consultation with the Pyrotechnic Special Effects Operator in charge.

• Whenever practical, pyrotechnic special effects should be hard wired from the effect to the firing system.
When remote control firing is planned, special precautions must be taken to prevent accidents, including but not limited to the following:  Having familiarity with the system being used and its limitations;  Performing a risk analysis in the event of premature firing or firing failure; and  Testing the firing system under the anticipated
conditions of use. **Safety on the Set After Use of Pyrotechnic Material** • After each pyrotechnic event, no one shall enter the pyrotechnic area other than the Pyrotechnic Special Effects Operator in charge, or his or her designated representative(s), until it is declared safe. This includes testing, rehearsals, and filming.
• Appropriate fire watch, as determined by the AHJ, should be maintained after each pyrotechnic event.
